To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a method to classify polar stratosphere nitric acid trihydrite (NAT) clouds into three size regimes and to detect the bottom of a cloud.
we developed a new method to detect PSC types, to subgroup them into size regimes, and to find their bottom altitude, based on radiative transfer simulations.

(1) the spectral peak in CRISTA-NF observations at 816  cm ^{−1} is caused by small NAT particles, (2) we developed a method that can detect and classify PSCs, (3) the method can detect the bottom altitude and the vertical extent of PSCs, and (4) during one local flight during the RECON-CILE campaign, we detected STS and medium NAT particles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of PSCs, especially NAT, from limb emission measurements, and it provides a new method to distinguish between NAT and STS.

the development and application of a new method to detect the presence and type of PSCs, to classify them into three size categories under the assumption of spheroidal particles, and to determine their bottom altitudes.
a new method to detect PSC types and their bottom altitudes from infrared limb emission observations, and we applied this method successfully to CRISTA-NF data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CRISTA-NB observations show that STS was present in the altitude range 17–20  km and that NAT particles were present in the altitude region 20–22  km with a median radius of about 3  µm.

the spectral peak at about 816  cm− 1 is caused by a mixture of NAT particles with a medium size and STS, and a peak at about 819  cm−1 by small NAT particles, which was also confirmed in a case study of a flight in the Arctic winter 2009.
the CRISTA-NB observations of the 816  cm −1 spectral feature in the PSCs are consistent with medium-sized NAT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a combination of different spectral indices can be used to detect and classify different types of PSCs, which can also be applied to other instruments.
we present a method to detect and to classify PSCs by their type and size based on radiative transfer simulations.

the new method can be applied to CRISTA-NF data and that the method is promising for other instruments, such as the Atmospheric Chemistry Experiment (ACE) Fourier transform spectrometers (FTS), the Michelson Interferometer for Passive Atmospheric Sounding (MIPAS), and the High-Resolution Dynamics Limb Sounder (HIRDLS).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spectral feature at about 816 cm−1 is a good indicator for the presence of NAT particles and can be used to detect the bottom of the cloud.
the combination of the colour indices and the CI method can be a powerful tool to detect and classify PSCs in observations.
the spectral feature in the 810-820  cm−2 can be used to detect and characterise NAT particles in PSCs.
